tagged_preview: <f=1>**2****8****th**** ****Meeting of the Wiesbaden Group on Business Registers****
<f=2>Name of the author(s): KUREMATSU Ryosuke, TANABE Tatsuya
Organization: Statistical Business Register Management Division, Statistics Bureau in Japan</f=2>
<f=4>Session 6: New Data sources: Opportunity and challenges </f=4>
<f=7>**Efforts for ****F****urther Development and Enhancement of Statistical Business Register in Japan**</f=7>

<f=12>The Statistical Business Register in Japan (JSBR) is maintained by using the data obtained from statistical surveys such as the Economic Census as the main source of data, and by additionally utilizing administrative data.</f=12>

<f=13>There was a discussion regarding the coverage of the JSBR: whether the JSBR comprehensively covers the business establishments in Japan as a whole, or whether the JSBR exhaustively covers small business establishments among the main sources of data obtained through statistical surveys. Thanks to building up the system of the corporate numbers in Japan, which are a kind of administrative data, in 2013 in Japan, the 2019 Economic Census was carried out by adding approximately 1.6 million new corporations to the census list. The comparison between the data of JSBR and the corporate number disclosure website was conducted with the name and addresses of corporations. As a result, the coverage of JSBR has been greatly expanded. However, since the enumerators only checked the activity status of the business establishments in operation from the outside appearance, it has become a new issue to improve the frequency of updating the basic data of the business establishments in operation in the JSBR.</f=13>

<f=14>Therefore, starting from 2023, basic data such as sales and the number of workers will be checked online and by mail every year within the scope that covers the top 90% of sales of business establishments in Japan, which will improve the frequency of updating the basic items of the JSBR.</f=14>

<f=15>Consequently, since the data on major business establishments and enterprises in the JSBR will be kept updated every year in a timely manner, it is expected to contribute to providing the most up-to-date population data of business establishments and enterprises, which results in improving the accuracy of various economic statistics and alleviating the burden on the respondents of statistical surveys through overlapping corrections.</f=15>
<f=18>_Keywords: __Economic Census, Coverage, Corporate Number, Establishment__ in Operation__, Update Frequency_</f=18>

<f=15>Early-onset neonatal sepsis (EOS) is associated with serious adverse outcomes. Current screening for clinical signs of sepsis in England typically involves one of two approaches: guidelines issued by the National Institute of Clinical Excellence (NICE) or a risk-based tool developed in the United States (US), the Kaiser Permanente Sepsis Risk Calculator (KP SRC). An update to the 2012 NICE guidelines in April 2021 permitted the alternative use of the KP SRC with prospective audit1. The application of the KP SRC has been consistently shown to reduce antibiotic usage2,3, however, uncertainty exists among clinicians as to whether this comes at the expense of increasing numbers of missed EOS cases. As such, benefits in reducing unnecessary treatment must be considered against potential undertreatment. Differences among NHS neonatal units in England arising from the co-existence of the two clinical screening protocols presents an opportunity to compare their performance to inform future guidance, especially important considering the limited but growing evidence base for the KP SRC outside the US. </f=15>

<f=16>To inform future assessments on the effectiveness of the KP SRC relative to NICE guidelines, we undertook a survey, disseminated via regional NHS Neonatal Operational Delivery Networks, to describe the implementation of current screening approaches in hospitals. Responses were received in August 2021 with follow-up of non-responders continuing until March 2022. A total of 72 acute hospital trusts responded to our survey (72/110, 65%), representing 60% (91/151) of neonatal units in hospitals across England. </f=16>

<f=17>The most common approach to the screening of EOS at the time of the survey was using NICE guidance (51/91 hospitals; 56%), with 23 hospitals reporting use of the new 2021 guidelines (Table 1). Just under a third of hospitals reported having adopted the KP SRC (28/91; 31%). Of the 59 hospitals who confirmed practice changes in the past 5 years, 22 changed from NICE guidelines to the KP SRC; 7 of these hospitals had specifically changed to KP SRC since January 2021. </f=17>

<f=18>There was marked geographical variation in management, with most hospitals in the North of England following NICE guidelines and those following KP SRC clustered in the South and West Midlands. No hospitals in the North of England who responded to the survey (n=29) reported adopting the KP SRC approach. Our results indicate that KP SRC was most frequently adopted by hospitals in the West Midlands (57%), South West (56%) and London (55%), although the low survey coverage in some regions introduces some uncertainty around these geographical differences. </f=18>

<f=19>In summary, we found that approximately one-third of hospitals in England were following the KP SRC and two-thirds NICE guidance, with marked geographical variation. Our findings highlight the need to develop an evidence-base to optimise clinical practice. The information gathered through our survey will be of benefit to future studies evaluating the impact of EOS screening protocols on health outcomes for these at-risk newborns.</f=19>
